articleTitle: Ring cameras go mobile as Amazon debuts AI-powered security drone and robot
summary: Amazon announced the Ring Drone Cam and Ring Rover Cam, mobile security devices that use AI Pilot, device cameras, on-device sensors and cloud processing to map indoor spaces and navigate patrol routes, with targeted availability on January 27, 2027, and scheduled shipping on December 16, 2026, respectively. The article examines operating limitations and privacy concerns, including cloud video storage, encryption criticized by the Electronic Frontier Foundation, and Ring’s history of employee access to recordings and compromised customer accounts.

deviceA.name: Ring Drone Cam
specs: Indoor flying security camera.
148-degree field of view.
360-degree rotation.
2K video resolution.
Two LED lights activate in low-light conditions.
8 minutes of flight time on a new, fully-charged battery under controlled conditions.
Includes a docking station for charging.
AI Pilot uses device cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors and cloud processing.
Maps indoor floor plans after the customer carries the drone through the spaces.
AI Pilot can supposedly identify rooms, suggest patrol points, plan routes and navigate around obstacles.
Set-route and scheduled operation described for Amazon Ring Protect subscribers.
Can automatically follow set routes in response to a notification from a Ring camera, sensor or alarm.
Can be controlled directly from Alexa Home Map.
Navigation may degrade around reflective surfaces such as polished marble or wet tile, featureless blank matte walls, and transparent surfaces such as frameless glass and mirrors.
Physical dimensions, charging duration, numerical coverage area and an explicit floor-count restriction are not stated in the supplied article.
deviceA.availability: Amazon aims for January 27, 2027, subject to Federal Communications Commission authorization; customers can register for email updates through the product page.

deviceB.name: Ring Rover Cam
specs: Wheeled autonomous security robot marketed for business.
Livestreams and records in up to 4K video resolution while patrolling or performing a 360-degree scan at a designated location.
Videos triggered by doorbell rings, motion events and Live View events are stored in the cloud for up to 180 days for sharing and replaying.
AI Pilot uses device cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors and cloud processing.
Maps indoor floor plans through autonomous exploration.
Can automatically respond to connected Ring device alerts by following preprogrammed patrol points.
Designed only for a single-floor, indoor environment; lacks stair-climbing capability.
Not compatible with curved edges, sunken areas, flooring transitions greater than 1.375 inches (3.5 centimeters), or black glossy floors.
Automatically adjustable mast allows viewing over counters, shelving and other obstacles.
Claimed coverage of up to 5,000 square feet (465 square meters).
Includes a siren, light tower and microphone for two-way audio communication.
Physical dimensions, mast height, battery runtime and charging duration are not stated in the supplied article.

coreControversy.corporateClaim: Amazon describes Ring Robotics as offering “privacy and security without compromise,” citing LED indicators and screen notifications when video and audio recordings are active. Amazon says videos from both devices will be protected with Throw Away the Key Encryption, introduced in September 2026.
coreControversy.criticismOrAlarm: The Electronic Frontier Foundation describes Throw Away the Key Encryption as an improvement over Ring’s former default settings but still well short of end-to-end encryption. EFF also criticizes Ring founder Jamie Siminoff’s “surveillance-first-privacy-last” approach, including reintroduced features allowing law enforcement to request footage or live-stream access from users’ home security devices. Ryan Calo previously described flying security cameras as creating new ways to surveil others indoors and giving companies greater access to potentially sensitive or identifying details of homes and businesses.
coreControversy.regulatoryOrHistoricalPrecedent: In a 2023 Federal Trade Commission investigation, Ring was charged with allowing employees and contractors to watch recordings of customers’ private spaces; the FTC also described inadequate safeguards that allowed hackers to access 55,000 US customers’ accounts. The earlier Ring Always Home Cam, temporarily available by invitation in September 2021, also prompted expanded privacy concerns. Since December 2025, fixed Ring doorbell camera owners have been able to enable Familiar Faces facial recognition, which is already the subject of a class action lawsuit. The new Ring Drone still requires Federal Communications Commission authorization before sale.

hiddenCatchesAndLimits: AI Pilot explicitly uses cloud processing alongside device cameras, specialized vision models and on-device sensors; it is not described as local-only.
Both devices digitally map the customer’s home or business floor plan during setup.

The drone’s set-route and scheduled operation is described for Amazon Ring Protect subscribers; the article does not specify a subscription price or separately establish the Rover’s subscription requirements.
The Ring Drone cannot go on sale before Federal Communications Commission authorization; January 27, 2027, is a conditional target.
Drone flight time is limited to 8 minutes under the stated new, fully-charged battery and controlled-condition assumptions.
Drone navigation may degrade near polished marble, wet tile, featureless blank matte walls, frameless glass and mirrors.
The Rover operates only indoors on a single floor and cannot climb stairs.
The Rover is incompatible with curved edges, sunken areas, flooring transitions greater than 1.375 inches (3.5 centimeters), and black glossy floors.
Rover coverage of up to 5,000 square feet (465 square meters) is an Amazon product-description claim.
Rover videos triggered by doorbell rings, motion events and Live View events are stored in the cloud for up to 180 days.
EFF says Throw Away the Key Encryption remains well short of end-to-end encryption; the article does not state encryption-key retention or deletion timing.
The article does not state a separate cloud video retention period for the drone.

The article reports no current mention of facial recognition or similar person-identification technologies in the new Ring Robotics products; this is not an assurance that such features cannot be introduced.
The Familiar Faces class action concerns fixed Ring doorbell cameras, not a facial-recognition feature established for either new robot.
